items.prompt: Why are the eggs of cliff-nesting birds so sharply pointed at one end?

options.label: They roll in a tight circle
options.feedback: A nudge sends the egg round, not over the edge.

options.label: They fit more snugly together
options.feedback: Guillemots lay a single egg. There is nothing to pack.

options.label: The chick hatches more easily
options.feedback: The chick breaks out at the blunt end either way.

options.label: They are stronger against impact
options.feedback: A round egg resists pressure better than a pointed one.

items.ok_line: A pointed egg pivots. A round one keeps going.
items.ko_line: Picture the egg being knocked on a bare ledge with no nest around it.
items.exp_title: The shape of a bare ledge
items.exp_text: A guillemot lays one egg straight onto rock, with no nest and no rim. Knocked, a rounded egg rolls in a straight line and is lost; the guillemot's is sharply tapered, so it pivots around its own point and comes back. Birds that nest in deep cups lay almost spherical eggs — nothing there is going anywhere. The shape is a reading of the place the bird chose.

items.prompt: What is an egg shell made of?

options.label: Calcium carbonate
options.feedback: The same mineral as chalk and limestone.

options.label: Hardened keratin
options.feedback: That is beak and feather, not shell.

options.label: A form of thin bone
options.feedback: Bone is living tissue. A shell is not.

options.label: Dried protein alone
options.feedback: Protein binds the shell, but the hardness is mineral.

items.ok_line: Chalk, essentially, laid down in a few hours.
items.ko_line: It dissolves in vinegar. That narrows it down.
items.exp_text: The shell is about 95% calcium carbonate on a protein mesh, and a hen lays down some two grams of it in roughly twenty hours — enough that a laying bird strips calcium from her own bones and must eat grit to replace it. It is not airtight: thousands of microscopic pores let the chick breathe while holding water in. Drop an egg in vinegar and the mineral dissolves, leaving the mesh as a rubbery bag.

options.label: A hard point for breaking the shell
options.feedback: It sits on the beak and drops off soon after hatching.

options.label: The first real tooth of a chick
options.feedback: No bird grows teeth at any age.

options.label: A ridge inside the shell
options.feedback: It belongs to the chick, not to the egg.

options.label: The point the parent pecks open
options.feedback: The chick does its own breaking out.

items.ok_line: A single-use tool, discarded once the job is done.
items.ko_line: Despite the name, it is not a tooth and it does not last.
items.exp_text: The chick grows a hard white point on top of its beak and uses it to chip a ring around the blunt end of the shell — where an air pocket has formed, giving it a first breath partway through. Breaking out can take a day or more, and helping usually kills the chick. The point falls off or is absorbed within days. Crocodiles and turtles hatch with the same device, arrived at quite separately.

items.prompt: Which living bird lays the largest egg?

options.label: The ostrich
options.feedback: About 1.4 kg, the weight of two dozen hen's eggs.

options.label: The emperor penguin
options.feedback: Around 460 g, large but far from the biggest.

options.label: The albatross
options.feedback: Its wings are enormous; its egg is not.

options.label: The emu
options.feedback: Around 600 g, and dark green — but still second.

items.ok_line: The largest egg, and the smallest relative to its layer.
items.ko_line: The heaviest bird alive lays the heaviest egg.
items.exp_title: Biggest egg, smallest for its bird
items.exp_text: An ostrich egg weighs around 1.4 kg with a shell some 2 mm thick, strong enough to take an adult's weight. Yet measured against its layer it is the smallest of any bird — barely 1.5% of her body. A kiwi turns that round completely: its egg reaches a quarter of the female's weight, so crammed inside that she can barely eat in the days before laying. The extinct elephant bird's egg held about nine litres.

items.prompt: What does a cuckoo do instead of raising its own young?

options.label: It lays its eggs in other birds' nests
options.feedback: The host raises a chick that is not its own.

options.label: It leaves the eggs to warm in the sun
options.feedback: Sunlight cannot hold a steady temperature for weeks.

options.label: It shares one nest with several pairs
options.feedback: Some birds do nest communally. The cuckoo does not.

options.label: It buries the eggs in warm sand
options.feedback: Turtles do that. No cuckoo does.

items.ok_line: The whole cost of raising the chick is passed to someone else.
items.ko_line: The eggs are incubated properly — just not by their mother.
items.exp_text: A female cuckoo watches a host's nest, waits for it to be left, and lays in seconds — removing one host egg so the count still looks right. Her lineage matches one host species and mimics its eggs closely. The cuckoo chick hatches early and heaves the remaining eggs over the rim, then is fed alone by foster parents often a fraction of its size. Around a hundred bird species live this way.

items.prompt: Why are the eggs of ground-nesting birds usually speckled?

options.label: The pattern hides them among stones
options.feedback: Broken outlines are much harder to see than plain ones.

options.label: The marks let heat in faster
options.feedback: The parent's body does the warming, not the sun.

options.label: They show the parent which way up
options.feedback: Birds turn eggs constantly; there is no fixed way up.

options.label: They make the shell stronger
options.feedback: The pigment is a surface layer and adds no strength.

items.ok_line: A blotched egg on gravel is astonishingly hard to pick out.
items.ko_line: Ask what a plain white egg would look like lying on open shingle.
items.exp_text: An egg laid on shingle or sand has no cover, so the shell does the hiding: blotches and streaks break up its outline until the eye slides past. Birds nesting in dark holes have no such need and lay plain white eggs, which they can find in the gloom. There is a second use — some species read their own speckle pattern to spot an intruder's egg, which is exactly what the cuckoo has to defeat.

options.label: All the eggs of one laying
options.feedback: Laid over days, then incubated together.

options.label: The nest and its lining
options.feedback: That is simply the nest.

options.label: All the chicks that survive
options.feedback: Those are the brood, once hatched.

options.label: The pair that share a nest
options.feedback: That is the breeding pair.

items.ok_line: One clutch, one round of laying.
items.ko_line: The word is about the eggs, and about one laying in particular.
items.exp_text: A clutch is the set of eggs laid in a single breeding attempt — usually one a day until the bird stops. Most delay incubation until the last is laid so the chicks hatch together; owls and some raptors start at once, so the eldest is far larger and, in a poor year, eats its siblings. Size varies enormously: an albatross lays one egg every two years, a partridge can lay twenty in a fortnight.

items.prompt: How do megapodes keep their eggs warm without sitting on them?

options.label: They bury them in rotting vegetation
options.feedback: The heap ferments, and the heat does the incubating.

options.label: They cover them with warm feathers
options.feedback: Loose feathers hold no heat without a body under them.

options.label: They leave them in direct sunlight
options.feedback: Sun swings from scorching to cold overnight.

options.label: They breathe warm air over them
options.feedback: No bird could keep that up for two months.

items.ok_line: A compost heap, and the male reads its temperature all season.
items.ko_line: The heat has to be steady for weeks. Only one of these could manage that.
items.exp_text: Megapodes of Australia and the islands build mounds of leaf litter and sand — some four metres across and weighing tonnes. Decay inside generates steady warmth, and the male tests it by pushing his beak in, then adds or scrapes away material to hold it near 33 °C for months. The chick digs its own way out fully feathered and can fly the same day. It never meets its parents.

items.prompt: Why does a sitting bird turn its eggs several times a day?

options.label: To stop the embryo sticking to the shell
options.feedback: Left still, it fuses to the membrane and dies.

options.label: To share the warmth of the nest evenly
options.feedback: The parent's body already covers the whole clutch.

options.label: To check that none has cracked
options.feedback: A bird can see a cracked egg without moving it.

options.label: To keep the shell from drying out
options.feedback: Turning does nothing about moisture loss.

items.ok_line: Stop turning and the embryo glues itself to the shell.
items.ko_line: The reason is inside the egg, not around it.
items.exp_title: An embryo that must not settle
items.exp_text: Inside the egg the embryo floats against the inner membrane, and if it rests in one position too long it adheres and stops developing. Turning keeps it clear and spreads the nutrients of the yolk around it. Some birds turn a clutch dozens of times a day, nudging with the beak. Incubators are built with a motor that does nothing else — without it, hatch rates collapse.

items.prompt: Which bird weaves the most elaborate hanging nest?

options.label: The weaver
options.feedback: It ties real knots in grass, working with beak and feet.

options.label: The swan
options.feedback: A heap of reeds at the water's edge, and nothing more.

options.label: The eagle
options.feedback: A huge platform of sticks, but never woven.

options.label: The gull
options.feedback: A scrape lined with a little grass.

items.ok_line: Real knots, tied by a bird with no hands.
items.ko_line: Look for the bird whose name says what it does.
items.exp_text: A male weaver strips grass into strips and knots them around a twig, holding one end in his foot and threading with his beak, until a hollow ball hangs with its entrance underneath — awkward for a snake to enter. He builds several and displays at each; a female inspects them and, if unimpressed, he tears the nest down and starts again. Sociable weavers go further and raise one thatched mass housing a hundred pairs, used for generations.
